_what: Real exposures of distant solar-system objects for the find-the-moving-object game, fetched from the telescope archives and aligned on the stars by scripts/fetch_game_sequences.py, with the object's position in every frame computed from the Minor Planet Center's records (or, for nights it has no positions from, JPL Horizons' orbit fitted to them) and checked against the pixels. Frames are greyscale, or true colour where 'colour' says which filter went into each channel.
_positions: Pixels in the saved frame: origin at the top-left corner, x right, y down, pixel centres at +0.5. times are mid-exposure, UT.

rounds.frames_are: colour composites: one exposure in each of g, r and i, taken within 5 minutes of each other and shown as blue, green and red (times are their mean)

colour.balance: each filter scaled to AB flux by Pan-STARRS1 photometry of the stars in its first exposure (zero points g 27.20 from 31 stars, r 27.12 from 43 stars, i 26.62 from 49 stars), so a source of flat spectrum is white; one asinh stretch of their mean, each channel keeping its share

skipped.why: set aside for its timing: its frames come in two short runs a day apart, minutes between frames within a night, so the object barely moves for most of the round and then leaps across the frame
set aside for objects that move further: its only night with many exposures (MegaCam, 14 April 2015, 60 s each over 1.5 hours) shows it cross 4% of a frame even at 0.14 arcseconds a pixel

set aside for objects that move further: on its discovery night (OSSOS, 13 April 2015, five 300-s MegaCam exposures over 3.4 hours) it crosses 6% of a frame at the camera's own scale, and at a scale fine enough for 10% it is lost in the noise; its other runs of nights (April 2015, March 2016) leave no frame that lies on one CCD in every exposure

set aside for objects that move further: on its discovery night (OSSOS, 17 May 2015, five 300-s MegaCam exposures) it crosses 5% of a frame, and its other nights that month are single exposures or 40-s DECam ones in which it is too faint to see

on the second of its two nights in the CFHT Legacy Survey (28 and 29 October 2003, five 500-s g exposures each) the dithered exposures put it at the edge of one CCD or the next, so no frame lies on one CCD in every exposure; the first night alone (35 minutes) shows it move about two seconds of arc

its only runs of nights with colour are the Dark Energy Survey's supernova fields: in September 2016 cloud and then the full moon hide it, and in August 2017 one visit a night has it on a CCD (g, r and i on 21, 26 and 31 August), five days apart, and its drift of four arcminutes south over those ten days does not fit in a frame that lies on one CCD in all of them

on the second of its two nights with DECam before dawn (14 and 16 July 2024, when it moved east) every exposure has it in a gap between CCDs, which leaves one night of four 50-s exposures in 25 minutes

too faint to follow by eye: on its three discovery nights (the HiTS survey, 17 to 19 February 2015, ten 86-s DECam g exposures) the computed positions agree with the pixels to half a pixel, but it stands only five to nine times above the noise in each, a speck among the field's faint galaxies

too faint to follow by eye: the archive's only runs of nights with it in the frame are a standard-star field's 15-s DECam exposures (g, r and i on six nights from 29 July 2019, and again in February 2020), and with all three filters added it stands two to five times above the noise

too faint to follow by eye: its discovery night's nine 287-s MegaCam exposures (OSSOS, 29 September 2013) show it at r = 24 to 25, three to four times the noise in each, and most are too far apart in time to add

too faint to follow by eye: on its best-covered night (10 October 2013, thirteen 330-s DECam z exposures in a Dark Energy Survey supernova field) it stands two to five times above the noise even with exposures added in pairs, and its track runs past a brighter galaxy
too faint to follow by eye: its discovery night (18 February 2015, five 86-s DECam g exposures of the HiTS survey, 1.6 hours apart) shows it at g = 24, four to five times the noise in each
too faint to follow by eye: on 17 May 2015 (five 300-s MegaCam exposures, OSSOS) it is at r = 24.5 to 25, about three times the noise in each

its discovery night (26 March 2014) has only three DECam exposures; the archive's other nights with five or more in one filter (DECam, March 2016) last twenty minutes, in which it moves under three pixels, and the MPC has no positions from them
the Dark Energy Survey imaged it once or twice a night, each time in a different filter (21 October 2014: r, i, z, z), so no night has five exposures in one filter
